strengths: Fills a genuine gap: no prior benchmark targets conceptual/analytical computer architecture reasoning; Table 1's positioning against software/hardware benchmarks is clear and fair.

Substantial construction effort: 2,671 QAs from three complementary sources (synthetic, exam parsing, crowdsourcing/competitions), each expert-reviewed; the crowdsourcing portal with LLM-difficulty scoring (Appendix B.1) is a thoughtful design that discourages overfitting to frontier models.

The LLM-as-a-judge validation (Sec 4.4) is a genuine strength: 11 human experts grading 908 responses, quantified 85.35% judge-human agreement versus 90.7% human-human agreement, plus tie-break frequency analysis and an alternative judge comparison (Gemini 2.5 Pro at 84.73%).

Comprehensive evaluation: 26 models across skills, topics, and modalities; the Recall vs. Reasoning split usefully separates 'don't know' from 'can't reason', and the GPT-5 vs. non-reasoning GPT-5 comparison (23-34% lifts on higher-order skills vs 3% on recall) is an informative finding.

Failure-mode analysis with worked examples (Appendix C) is high quality and diagnostic; e.g., the short-circuit-evaluation side-channel and cache-coherence granularity examples are convincing demonstrations of the architecture-semantics gap.
Ethics and reproducibility statements are thorough, including licensing, contributor consent, LLM usage disclosure, and full prompt templates in Appendix D.
weaknesses: Key taxonomy labels (skill, topic) are produced by LLM classification without human audit of label accuracy. The headline design/implement claims rest on very small subsets (Design: 35 QAs, Implement: 77 QAs per Fig. 5); no confidence intervals are reported, so claims like 'design skills exhibit the widest performance gaps, ranging between 18-87%' carry large uncertainty that the paper does not propagate.

Possible data contamination is never addressed: many exam QAs come from publicly accessible university course pages, and QUARCH-RECALL scores are saturated (83-89%), consistent with these items appearing in pretraining corpora. Recall performance being near-ceiling may therefore overstate how much 'domain knowledge is present' versus memorized. Some form of contamination check or discussion is needed.

The LLM judge (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) is also one of the evaluated models, and 85.35% agreement means ~15% of FRQ verdicts disagree with expert consensus. FRQs are 1,124/2,671 (~42%) of the benchmark, so judge noise could affect model rankings, especially between close models (e.g., Claude Sonnet 4 vs. Claude 3.7 Sonnet Thinking). The validation set is also modest: 100 FRQs and one response per model.

Implementation questions are graded by an LLM judge against written solutions rather than by execution-based validation; a code answer judged 'correct' may not actually run, which weakens the validity of the Implement split relative to existing execution-verified hardware benchmarks the paper itself cites (VerilogEval, CVDP).

Headline comparison in Figure 1 mixes QUARCH results with third-party reported numbers from Vals AI on other benchmarks, without controlling for evaluation protocol differences (sampling, prompting, judge methodology), making the cross-benchmark gap qualitative at best.

Presentation inconsistencies: conflicting GPT-5 configurations across tables ('GPT-5' vs 'GPT-5 (High Effort)' in Tables 5-6 vs Table 2) without clear reconciliation; figures referenced out of order (Fig. 5 before Fig. 4); placeholder captions ('Caption for image 1/2') in Appendix C.1.4; a stray comma after a citation in Sec 2.2.
Only n=3 generations per question; fine-grained per-topic claims (e.g., Llama 4 vs Mistral topic specialization in Insight 4) are drawn from small per-topic cell counts with no significance testing.

strengths: Fills a genuine gap: no existing benchmark targets architectural (as opposed to code-artifact) reasoning, and the paper makes this case convincingly in Sec. 1 and Table 1, positioning QUARCH against SWE-bench, RTL/EDA, and QA benchmarks along meaningful axes.

Substantial and diverse data collection effort: 2,671 QAs from three complementary sources (synthetic generation, exam parsing, expert crowdsourcing with an interactive portal), with 140+ contributors across 40 institutions; this is a serious community contribution that is hard to replicate.

Above-average rigor on the LLM-as-a-judge question: the 908-response human validation study (Sec. 4.4) with 11 domain experts, majority consensus, and comparison of Claude 3.7 (85.35%) vs Gemini 2.5 Pro (84.73%) judges, plus per-judge tie-breaking statistics over 65,659 responses, directly addresses the main validity concern for FRQ grading.

Broad evaluation coverage (26 models spanning frontier, open, and small models) with consistent findings (recall mastered at 83–89%, higher-order skills much weaker; ~23–30 point gains from GPT-5 reasoning on analyze/design/implement vs 3% on recall) that are plausible and actionable.

The failure-mode analysis (Sec. 4.3, Appendix C) with worked examples of incorrect frontier responses (reuse intervals, timing side channels from short-circuit evaluation, coherence state tracking) is genuinely insightful and diagnostic, going beyond aggregate scores.
Ethics and LLM-usage statements are unusually thorough and honest (consent for contributors, licensing, explicit LLM usage disclosure).
weaknesses: The Design split appears to contain only ~35 questions and Implement ~77 (Figure 5), yet the paper draws strong conclusions from them ('design skills exhibit the widest performance gaps, ranging 18-87%', 'strong discriminative signal'). Per-skill accuracies computed on 35 items carry very large binomial uncertainty, and no confidence intervals or variance estimates are reported anywhere in the paper, despite models differing by only a few points on adjacent metrics.

No contamination analysis or mitigation is discussed. Exam questions are sourced from 'publicly accessible university course pages' and synthetic items from an open public corpus — exactly the material frontier LLMs are trained on. For a benchmark whose headline claim is that models fail these questions, measuring (rather than assuming) contamination is essential, and the QUARCH-RECALL near-saturation is consistent with memorization rather than knowledge.

A conflict of interest in grading: Claude 3.7 Sonnet Thinking is both the LLM judge for all FRQ evaluations and one of the evaluated student models. Even with the 85.35% human agreement rate, ~15% judge error is larger than the gap separating mid-table models (e.g., 52.1 vs 56.8), so rank ordering of several models is not distinguishable from judge noise; there is also no per-model-family bias analysis of the judge.

Skill and topic labels are assigned purely by LLM labeling (Appendix D.4, D.5) without any reported human validation of label accuracy, yet the entire QUARCH-RECALL vs QUARCH-REASONING dichotomy — the paper's central evaluation axis — rests on these labels.

Internal inconsistencies: Figure 1 (sourced from a third party, Vals AI) shows GPT-5 at ~77-80% on QuArch Reasoning while Table 2 reports 72.4; mixing externally reported numbers with the authors' own protocol in the motivating figure undermines comparability of the headline gap claim.

The 'first benchmark' claim is stated strongly; given adjacent prior work (CodeMMLU, CVDP, EDA Corpus) it should be scoped more carefully. The skills taxonomy itself is essentially a Bloom-style classification and offers limited methodological novelty.

Reproducibility is incomplete: prompts are provided, but the manuscript does not explicitly commit to releasing the dataset, evaluation harness, or judge outputs under a fixed version, which is critical for a benchmark intended as a community standard. Minor but telling sloppiness (e.g., a leftover 'you will not be paid' artifact in the judge prompt, Appendix D.3) further weakens confidence in evaluation hygiene.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and clearly articulated gap: no existing LLM benchmark targets conceptual/analytical reasoning in computer architecture, as distinct from code generation (SWE-bench, VerilogEval) or chip-implementation tasks. Table 1 positions the contribution carefully against related work.

The construction methodology is substantive and multi-pronged (synthetic generation, crowdsourcing/competitions, academic exams), with every QA expert-validated by doctoral-level domain experts. The community scale (140+ contributors, 40 institutions) and the crowdsourcing portal with LLM-testing feedback (Appendix B.1) are impressive infrastructure contributions.

The LLM-as-a-judge validation is unusually rigorous for a benchmark paper: 11 domain experts graded 908 FRQ responses, with an 85.35% human-LLM agreement rate benchmarked against a 90.7% human-human agreement rate, plus tie-breaking analysis over 65,659 judgments (Appendix B.6). This materially strengthens confidence in the FRQ scoring.

The evaluation is broad (26 models) and the analysis is diagnostic rather than purely leaderboard-driven: the Recall/Analyze/Design/Implement split separates 'don't know' from 'can't reason', and the failure-mode analysis (architecture-semantics of code, state tracking, unconventional assumptions, modality sensitivity) is supported with concrete, well-annotated examples in the appendix.

Reproducibility and ethics are handled well: all prompts are documented in Appendix D, methodology is described in enough detail to replicate, and the ethics statement transparently covers sourcing, consent, and licensing.
weaknesses: Sample sizes for the higher-order skills are very small yet support headline claims. Figure 5 shows only ~35 Design and ~77 Implement QAs (vs. 1,564 Recall and 995 Analyze). Conclusions such as 'GPT-5 stands as an extreme outlier on design QAs at 89%' are drawn from these tiny subsets with no confidence intervals or significance testing anywhere in the paper. Given per-generation accuracy over only n=3 samples, several between-model gaps (e.g., Gemini 2.5 Pro 62.9 vs. Qwen3 235B Thinking 61.3) may not be statistically meaningful.

Data contamination is not addressed. A large fraction of the benchmark comes from public university exams and open web sources, and synthetic QAs are generated from publicly available corpora. Since the paper's central purpose is to measure frontier-model architectural reasoning over time (and the authors themselves cite MathArena as an uncontaminated benchmark), the absence of any contamination audit or mitigation is a significant omission for a benchmark intended to become a community standard.

Potential judge-family bias is not discussed. Claude 3.7 Sonnet (Thinking) is the judge for all evaluations while Claude Sonnet 4 and Claude 3.7 Sonnet Thinking are among the evaluated models, raising the possibility of self-family grading bias; the human validation study does not report agreement stratified by evaluated model family.

The skill/topic labels underpinning the analysis (e.g., skill-wise trends in Table 3, topic-wise radar plots in Figure 14) are produced by LLM labeling pipelines with limited reported validation of label accuracy. Label noise here would propagate directly into the paper's core findings about skill-level strengths and weaknesses.

Figure 1, used to motivate the entire paper, presents 'reported results (Vals AI, Inc., 2025)' — third-party numbers for QUARCH alongside other benchmarks evaluated under potentially different conditions, rather than a controlled side-by-side evaluation performed by the authors. Additionally, minor inconsistencies between Table 2 and Table 5 (e.g., 'GPT-5' vs. 'GPT-5 (High Effort)' with different Recall values: 89.0 vs. 86.4) are confusing and unexplained.

The benchmark is heavily skewed toward recall-style MCQs (1,547 cloze-derived MCQs vs. 1,124 FRQs, of which only ~100 are Design/Implement). The authors acknowledge this, but it weakens the framing of QUARCH-REASONING as a benchmark of 'higher-order thinking'; the reasoning portion is a minority of the dataset and its free-response evaluation depends entirely on the LLM judge.

Some claims of originality ('the first benchmark') are strong relative to overlapping resources (CodeMMLU, CVDP, EDA Corpus) — the Table 1 comparison helps, but the boundary between 'architecture reasoning' and 'code reasoning with architectural content' deserves more nuance.

strengths: Substantial and thoughtfully curated resource: 2,671 expert-validated QAs spanning 13 architecture topics, four skills (Recall/Analyze/Design/Implement), MCQ and FRQ formats, and multimodal items, with a clear skills framework grounded in educational competency taxonomies (Sec. 2.1)

Unusually careful validation of LLM-as-a-judge: agreement with 11 domain experts on 908 graded responses (85.48%) benchmarked against human-human agreement (90.75%), plus cross-judge consistency (~90% across three judges over ~80k responses) and a self-judgment bias analysis (Appendix B.9)

Genuine attempt to demonstrate utility beyond leaderboard numbers: knowledge-transfer case studies on memory-hierarchy and DRAM-controller design with simulator-based evaluation, including a positive correlation between QUARCH-REASONING accuracy and downstream design quality (r=0.726, p=0.007)
Strong attention to benchmark integrity: gated access, Fernet-encrypted ground truth, private hold-out set for leaderboard qualification, and permissive-source ethics statement (Appendix A, B.1)
Excellent reproducibility: all construction, filtering, grading, and case-study prompts are published in the appendix; fine-tuning hyperparameters and model lists are provided
Informative analysis of failure modes (architecture-semantics of code execution, implicit conventions, state tracking, modality sensitivity) with worked examples in the appendix
weaknesses: Severe skill imbalance undercuts the headline framing: of 2,671 QAs, only 42 are Design and 98 Implement (Sec. 2.3); the 'reasoning' signal that drives the paper's central conclusions rests on a small, skew-prone subset, and claims about its discriminative power ('small but high-quality benchmarks can meaningfully discriminate...') are asserted rather than quantified

The knowledge-transfer evidence is thin and partly cherry-picked: the SFT study uses only 45 filtered QAs and 676 samples, 20 trials per condition, and the reported 'up to 1.99x' area improvement comes from an aggressive config that simultaneously *reduces* success rate (35% vs 55% baseline for Llama; 50% vs 30% for Gemma), weakening the causal story that QUARCH fine-tuning (as opposed to more GPT-5.2-style didactic data) transfers; no control arm distills explanations from unrelated topics

Case Study #2's correlation is based on only ~12 model-workload points from 3 models, which is weak statistical support for the strong claim that 'improvement on QUARCH directly reflects improvement on computer architecture tasks'

Contamination risk is acknowledged but not measured: exam-derived QAs come from publicly accessible university course pages, and the publicly released portion of the benchmark could overlap pretraining corpora; no n-gram or embedding-based contamination audit against evaluated models is reported

Headline results lack uncertainty quantification: no confidence intervals or significance tests accompany Tables 2, 3, 6, 7, and the 3-sample per-generation accuracy protocol's variance is not analyzed

Judge fidelity has residual concerns: ~14.5% of judge verdicts disagree with expert consensus (Table 5), and the primary judge (Claude-3.7-Thinking) is itself among the evaluated student models; while self-bias was probed on a small subset (1/39 vs 7/24), the sample sizes are too small to be conclusive

Zero-shot-only evaluation limits the benchmark's characterization; no few-shot, retrieval-augmented, or tool-scaffolded baselines are explored despite the authors' argument that QUARCH complements agentic benchmarks

Possible under-claiming of novelty risk: 'first benchmark' claims should be more carefully delineated against adjacent conceptual-QA efforts (e.g., EDA Corpus, CVDP conceptual portions) covered in Table 1

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: no existing benchmark targets conceptual/analytical computer architecture reasoning (Table 1 positioning is well-motivated), and the dataset is substantial (2,671 QAs) with a multi-pronged construction pipeline (synthetic generation, exam parsing, expert crowdsourcing) that is thoroughly documented in the appendix.

The skills framework (Recall/Analyze/Design/Implement) is a sensible decomposition grounded in educational taxonomies, and per-skill results (Table 3) reveal interpretable findings, e.g., reasoning models gain little on recall but large gains on higher-order skills.

The LLM-as-a-judge validation (Sec. 4.5, Appendix B.9) is more rigorous than most benchmark papers: 908 responses graded by up to 3 of 11 domain experts, comparison against three candidate judge models, cross-judge agreement matrices, and a self-judgment bias analysis.

The knowledge-transfer case studies (memory hierarchy design with Timeloop/Accelergy; DRAM controller design with a simulator) attempt to connect QA benchmark scores to a concrete downstream design task, which is uncommon and valuable in principle.
Benchmark integrity measures (Fernet-encrypted ground truth, private hold-out set, gated access) and a detailed ethics statement are commendable.
weaknesses: The headline FRQ results rest on LLM-as-a-judge whose fidelity is only validated on a small sample (100 QAs, 908 responses) with 14.5% disagreement from human experts; the confusion matrix shows substantial asymmetric error (60 human-correct judged incorrect, 73 judge-correct human-incorrect), yet no analysis of whether these errors are systematic or bias model rankings. This undermines confidence in the central claims about model performance.

The higher-order skill claims rest on very small question counts (Design: 42, Implement: 98 per Figure 5), so per-skill accuracies in Table 3 carry high variance and are reported without confidence intervals or significance testing; claims like '23 of 30 models score lower on implement than design' are fragile at this sample size.

1,547 of 2,671 QAs are synthetically generated cloze-style MCQs that the authors themselves admit 'naturally involve little reasoning,' and exam QAs scraped from public university course pages carry nontrivial contamination risk that is only partially mitigated by the holdout set; no decontamination analysis against model pretraining data is reported.

The transfer study's evidence is weak: SFT on only 45 QAs / 676 samples with 20 trials per condition, and the 'up to 1.99x more area-efficient' claim comes from the best single configuration (Config 2), which actually reduced success rate (35% and 50% vs. baselines 55% and 30%). The DRAM controller correlation (r=0.726) is based on only 12 points (3 models x 4 workloads). These results are presented as headline abstract claims ('up to 1.99x', 'up to 40%') that overstate the robustness of the evidence.

All evaluations are zero-shot with a single generation setting (n=3); no few-shot, chain-of-thought prompting, or self-consistency baselines are explored, limiting what can be concluded about 'reasoning gaps' versus prompting sensitivity.

Presentation issues reduce trust: the paper inconsistently states '10 frontier models' vs. 11 in Table 2 (which lists 10 rows), the benchmark URL is literally missing from the text ('available at: .'), several tables have misaligned/typo-laden text (e.g., 'futhermore', 'disincentivize'), and Figure 1 cites a third-party leaderboard rather than the authors' own results.

The 'first benchmark' claim is repeated but not carefully defended against adjacent prior work (e.g., EDA Corpus, ArchGym, CacheMind), and the novelty is primarily a curated dataset rather than methodological insight; the failure-mode analysis in Sec. 4.3 is anecdotal, illustrated by hand-picked examples rather than quantified across the dataset.

strengths: Fills a genuine gap: no prior benchmark targets conceptual/analytical computer-architecture reasoning, and the paper positions QuArch carefully against adjacent software- and RTL-focused benchmarks (Table 1), making the novelty claim defensible.

The benchmark itself is substantial and well-characterized: 2,671 expert-validated QAs across 13 topics, four skills (Recall/Analyze/Design/Implement), and multiple modalities (548 multimodal QAs, 1,124 FRQs), with a clear three-pronged construction methodology (synthetic generation, exam parsing, crowdsourcing/competitions) that draws from artifacts used to train human architects.

The LLM-as-a-judge validation is unusually thorough for a benchmark paper: agreement with 11 domain experts on 908 graded responses (85.48% vs. 90.75% human-human agreement), cross-judge consistency over ~80,000 responses from three candidate judges, alternative-judge full result tables (Tables 11-12), and a self-judgment bias analysis (Claude FPR 2.6% vs. Gemini 29.2%). This materially strengthens trust in headline FRQ scores.

Benchmark integrity is taken seriously: gated access, Fernet-encrypted ground truth, a private hold-out subset for leaderboard qualification, and anti-leakage API agreements - a good template for domain benchmarks at contamination risk.

The knowledge-transfer case studies go beyond superficial claims: the main memory-hierarchy case study includes a control (fine-tuning on all unfiltered FRQs did not help), and Case Study #2 provides a statistically reported correlation (r=0.726, p=0.007) between QuArch-Reasoning accuracy and downstream DRAM controller energy efficiency, directly addressing the 'does QA performance matter' question.

Extensive evaluation coverage (30 models including SLMs and open-source models) with skill-, topic-, and modality-wise breakdowns, plus concrete failure-mode taxonomy (architecture-semantics of code, implicit conventions, state tracking, modality sensitivity) illustrated with detailed worked examples in Appendix C.

Reproducibility and ethics handling are solid: prompts for all construction/evaluation pipelines are included, hyperparameters for fine-tuning are listed, and the ethics statement addresses contributor consent, licensing, and takedown policy explicitly.
weaknesses: The knowledge-transfer evidence rests on small samples. Case Study #1 uses 20 trials per configuration with no confidence intervals or statistical tests on the success-rate gains (30%->70%, 55%->95%), and the headline '1.99x more area-efficient' result is a best-across-trials metric from Config 2, which simultaneously *reduces* success rate (95%->35% for Llama) - the trade-off is reported but the claim framing in the abstract underplays it.

The Design (42) and Implement (98) QAs are extremely small subsets, so per-skill accuracies in Table 3 (e.g., design accuracies varying from 26% to 79%) are noisy and model rankings within these skills may not be reliable. The paper acknowledges the imbalance but several conclusions (e.g., 'implement exhibits the widest gaps') are drawn from these small strata.

Judge choice noticeably affects absolute scores: e.g., GPT-5.2 scores 73.2 with the Claude judge but 79.4 with Gemini and 77.7 with Qwen (Tables 2, 11, 12). While cross-judge agreement is high, this variance suggests headline numbers carry a judge-dependent uncertainty that is not quantified as error bars in the main tables.

The correlation in Case Study #2 is based on only 12 model-workload points (3 models x 4 workloads) from 3 non-frontier-plus-frontier models; with n=12, r=0.726 is suggestive rather than conclusive, and confounds (model scale, tool-use ability) are not controlled.

Some contamination risk remains: exam-derived QAs from publicly accessible university course pages may already exist in pretraining corpora of the very frontier models evaluated; gating the released benchmark cannot retroactively address this, and the paper does not report a deduplication/canary check against training data.

Minor presentation issues: the judge prompt in Appendix D.3 contains an artifact ('you will not be paid for your work') inherited from a crowdsourced grading prompt; the abstract/Section 4.1 vacillate between '10 frontier models' and '11 models' (Table 2 lists 10); and the claim 'first benchmark' should be softened given partially overlapping items in CVDP and EDA Corpus.

The utility of the fine-tuning result is bounded: it uses only 45/2,671 QAs filtered by another LLM and distilled from GPT-5.2, so it demonstrates transfer for a narrow slice of QuArch content rather than validating the benchmark broadly; the case-study success could partly reflect task-specific prompt/format effects rather than architectural knowledge per se.
